messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 62-year-old Latin American surgeon, has experienced significant distress since a life-threatening accident in which he was involved in a severe car crash. The event left him with deep emotional scars that have affected his daily life and work. On the day of the accident, Carlos was driving home from the hospital after completing an emergency surgery late into the night. As he navigated through the rain-soaked streets, another vehicle lost control on a slippery curve and crashed directly into his car. The impact was violent and sudden, leaving Carlos dazed and struggling to escape the wreckage as the other car’s engine ignited in flames. Since then, known people who were related to the event—emergency responders and fellow surgeons who witnessed the aftermath of the crash—trigger intense distress for him. Even a specific texture associated with the accident—a gritty, charred material that clung to his clothing post-crash—becomes unbearable when he encounters it in various contexts. The vividness and realness of his memories are overwhelming; they intrude unbidden, leaving Carlos feeling as though he is reliving the event. He often finds himself pushing these intrusive thoughts away before fully processing them, only for them to return with renewed intensity later. These memories, more real than any ordinary recollection, contribute significantly to his distress. In response to this overwhelming memory and triggers, Carlos has adopted several maladaptive strategies that have gradually altered his daily life. He avoids situations that put physical stress on his body, such as running or even strenuous work in the hospital operating room. His avoidance extends beyond just physical stress; he gives up pleasant activities that once brought him joy, like playing soccer with friends and attending family gatherings. The thought of encountering a trigger during these events is too daunting to bear. One specific incident highlighted the extent of his avoidance behavior. During a routine check-up at a local clinic, Carlos encountered a doctor who had been present at the scene of the accident. This encounter triggered an intense panic attack, leading him to abruptly leave without completing the appointment. Since then, he has refrained from visiting that clinic and even avoids driving through the neighborhood where it is located. Carlos’s avoidance behaviors also extend to his professional life as a surgeon. He has become increasingly reluctant to perform surgeries involving high-risk patients, fearing that another stressful incident might trigger a relapse of his trauma symptoms. This has strained his relationship with colleagues who rely on his expertise and have noticed his withdrawal from complex cases. The cycle of avoidance has only deepened his distress. When he does engage in activities or encounters triggers—like the specific texture associated with the accident—it exacerbates his anxiety, leading him to further avoid these situations. This self-reinforcing loop has made it increasingly difficult for Carlos to maintain a semblance of normalcy in his daily life. Despite the profound impact on his personal and professional life, what finally brought Carlos to seek help was a realization that he could no longer ignore the emotional toll this trauma had taken. He is most afraid of losing control and becoming incapacitated by his symptoms, yet he hopes for relief from these overwhelming experiences and the ability to regain some semblance of normalcy in his life. Carlos’s journey towards recovery begins with acknowledging the need for support and understanding that his fear-driven behaviors have become a part of his daily existence. He is eager to explore ways to manage his triggers and memories, hoping to regain control over his life and return to the fulfilling career he once enjoyed.
